verses.1: Al-Mizan identifies Nūn as a disjointed letter and qalam as the ordinary writing implement; saṭr means a line, and yasṭurūn writing line by line. The oath apparently encompasses the pen and all writing, a divine blessing by which people communicate distant thoughts and traverse time and place, and for which they should be grateful. The commentary reports narrower interpretations—writing itself, the primordial pen and angelic scribes, the Guarded Tablet, or learned men and their writing—but judges them weak.
verses.2: Al-Mizan says bi-niʿmah either marks the cause of, or accompaniment with, the Lord’s grace in declaring the Prophet free of madness. The context makes that grace prophethood: a prophet cannot have an impairment that compromises communication of the indispensable guidance organizing human life. It therefore refutes the later quoted accusation of madness and comforts the Prophet. An alternate explanation makes the grace his eloquence, perfect intellect, conduct, freedom from defect, and every virtue; Al-Mizan judges the prophethood reading stronger.
verses.3: Al-Mizan takes mamnūn from the root meaning to cut or weaken, so the Prophet’s reward for messengership is unceasing and his efforts are not vain. It rejects the alternate sense, drawn from the other root denoting reminders of a favor, that the reward comes without burdening him with indebtedness. God is the true owner of every servant, attribute, act, and offered deed; whatever a servant has is His loan. Calling recompense a wage for effort is itself a further divine gift, while God alone may demand gratitude from every servant, including the Prophet.
verses.4: Al-Mizan defines khuluq as an inner spiritual disposition from which acts readily arise, noble or ignoble. Unlike khalq, which came to denote outward form, khulq denotes inward faculties perceived by intuition. The verse praises the Prophet’s personal and social conduct—justice, forbearance under harm, clemency, diligence, kindness, civility, and humility. It rejects interpreting khulq simply as religion or Islam unless that reading is made to encompass this moral reality.
verses.5: Al-Mizan makes the promise that the Prophet and his accusers will see who is mad the consequence of his prophethood, noble conduct, and divine reward: his mission will unveil the truth to them. It allows that this is shown both in this world, where the Prophet and his religion prevail, and in the hereafter, where opponents meet the consequences of their deeds. Maftūn normally means afflicted with madness, with bi- an extraneous connective, so each side will see whether the Prophet or his deniers is afflicted. The commentary also reports a grammatical reading in which maftūn is a verbal noun and bi- means “on,” yielding the question on which side the affliction falls.

verses.7: Al-Mizan says the preceding contrast makes the Prophet’s accusers the truly erring and afflicted, while the Prophet is guided; their respective states will become manifest. Since guidance belongs to God’s path, God knows best who has strayed from it and who follows it rightly.
verses.8: Al-Mizan treats the command as the necessary consequence of the prior verdict: the known body of rejecters are erring and afflicted, so the Prophet must not yield to them in either word or deed.
verses.9: Al-Mizan explains tudhin as softening toward the rejecters so as to seek a middle ground between religions; a reported offer was that the Prophet leave their gods alone and they would leave his. “They” includes all who reject him, while the following fa- indicates what would follow such pliancy, not its cause.
verses.10: Al-Mizan says the Prophet must not yield to the enemies of religion who press him to comply, because their catalogue of nine traits forms the sum of vice. The ḥallāf profanes oaths by swearing over everything; mahīn is low-minded; hammāz obsessively finds fault and slanders; and mashshāʾ bi-namīm carries tales to ruin relations. Mannāʿ lil-khayr blocks good or prevents it reaching those entitled to it; muʿtadī crosses into aggression; athīm is habitually sinful; and ʿutul is crude, obscene, hostile, and forceful in falsehood. Zanīm is variously explained as one of unknown or falsely claimed lineage, or one conspicuously marked by evil; these senses converge. The last two traits may be the worst, but in any case such a person must neither be obeyed in truth nor imitated.

verses.14: Al-Mizan takes possession of wealth and sons as the cause of the man’s arrogant denial of God’s blessings and consequent wickedness, rather than gratitude and self-reform. It reports the narrower reading that one must not obey him merely because he has wealth and children, but judges its own reading broader and closer. The following claim that revelation is ancient fables continues the explanation of the command not to yield to him.

verses.16: Al-Mizan explains wasm and simah as marking, and khurṭūm as nose; its use may sarcastically suggest an elephant’s trunk or pig’s snout. The verse is a severe threat to the enemies of God, His Messenger, and revelation. Branding the prominent nose evidently means an unmistakable, public humiliation, since the nose signifies both pride and disgrace.
verses.17: Al-Mizan explains balāʾ as trial, ṣurm as plucking fruit, ṭāʾif as a nocturnal encompassing punishment, and ṣarīm as either a plucked tree, blackened night, or barren sand-dune. Read with the preceding verses, the garden’s owners prefigure the Prophet’s rejecters: engrossed in wealth, children, and material causes, they neither thanked nor worshipped their Lord and faced sudden worldly punishment or the hereafter, when possessions could not help and regret could not avert chastisement. This reading assumes the verses were revealed together. A narration instead connects them to the Meccan drought after the Prophet prayed against the Quraysh, making balāʾ the drought; Al-Mizan notes that this does not fit the mutual blaming in (68:30). It identifies the garden owners as people of Yemen and reports that their story will appear in the narrations. Their oath to harvest either omitted “God willing,” thereby trusting material causes, or withheld the poor’s share. The nocturnal visitation left their garden stripped, charred black, or useless and barren.

verses.21: Al-Mizan explains that tanādaw is their morning call to one another, ṣārimīn their intention to pluck fruit rather than a completed harvest, and ḥirth their crops and orchard. They secretly consulted (yatakhāfatūn) to go early and keep every poor person from entering, lest the poor follow them and demand a share. Their going ʿalā ḥirdin qādirīn means that, capable of harvesting, they intended to prevent the poor from receiving any of it. Citing al-Kashshāf, the commentary adds that ighdū takes ʿalā because it carries the sense of turning toward, whereas it otherwise takes ilā.

verses.26: Al-Mizan says that, seeing the garden stripped bare by God, its owners recognize their wrong in seeking to harvest while excluding the poor. It reports the interpretation that “we have gone astray” means they took the wrong route to their garden, but takes their next statement as an escalation: they were not only wrong but deprived of their harvest.
verses.27: Al-Mizan says that, seeing the garden stripped bare by God, its owners recognize their wrong in seeking to harvest while excluding the poor. It reports the interpretation that “we have gone astray” means they took the wrong route to their garden, but takes their next statement as an escalation: they were not only wrong but deprived of their harvest.
verses.28: Al-Mizan takes awsaṭuhum as the most moderate-tempered of them because he recalled what was right, rejecting the reading that he was merely middlemost in age. His earlier admonition is omitted for brevity. His call to tasbīḥ means denying God partners: by resolving to harvest without saying “God willing,” they made themselves and material causes independent in causation, which is shirk. Acknowledging that success and failure depend on God’s will and permission affirms that the Divine Command has no partner. The commentary reports that tasbīḥ may instead mean remembrance and repentance for planning to exclude the poor, and considers this worthy if their earlier failure meant withholding the poor’s share.
verses.29: Al-Mizan says their tasbīḥ, prompted by the best man’s rebuke, now disavows the partners they had asserted by trusting their harvest to themselves and material causes. They confess that their Lord manages affairs by His will and that they wronged themselves through shirk. It also reports the reading that they repented for wronging both themselves and the poor.
verses.30: Al-Mizan says they then blamed one another for their wrongdoing.
verses.31: Al-Mizan explains ṭughyān as crossing the limits of servitude to God. The owners confess their shirk and failure to acknowledge His unity, then hope that, since they turn their humble petition solely to their Lord, He will replace their destroyed garden’s fruit with something better.
verses.32: Al-Mizan explains ṭughyān as crossing the limits of servitude to God. The owners confess their shirk and failure to acknowledge His unity, then hope that, since they turn their humble petition solely to their Lord, He will replace their destroyed garden’s fruit with something better.
verses.33: Al-Mizan says the garden owners’ punishment is a recurrent pattern. Tested with wealth and children, a person may see himself independent, make himself and material causes partners with God, commit evil heedless of its consequences, and be seized suddenly. He then remembers prior counsel, regrets, and begs for restored blessing. The chastisement of the hereafter is greater: issuing from divine power, it leaves no escape even by death or annihilation and, unlike worldly calamity, endures without end.
verses.34: Al-Mizan reads "with their Lord" (ʿinda rabbihim) as a mercy-filled bond between God and the reverent, earned by confining lordship to Him and worshipping sincerely. jannāt-i naʿīm are gardens whose bliss is unalloyed by pain or punishment; the commentary notes that naʿīm is explained elsewhere as wilāyah, allegiance to the Prophet and his family.
verses.35: Al-Mizan rejects the claim that the guilty will equal or surpass those who submit at the Resurrection. The verse's reversed comparison emphasizes the honor God gives those who submit, not an inequitable treatment of the two groups; islām is obedience to God's command in action and restraint from sin. The succeeding questions exhaust the possible grounds for the claim: reason, a revealed book, or a divine verbal promise offer none. Nor can the guilty secure equality by their own power, through associates, or by control of the unseen decree; perhaps they merely evade the Prophet's call as though it charged a fee, but that too is denied.
verses.36: Al-Mizan treats the question as astonishment at equating the guilty with those who submit on the Day of Resurrection; sound reason itself rejects such a judgment as delusion.
verses.37: Al-Mizan says the rhetorical question denies that their equality-claim has revelatory warrant. kitāb is a revealed scripture, tadrusūn means reading it, and takhayyarūn choosing: no divine book tells them they may choose whatever they want, including bliss, in the hereafter.
verses.38: Al-Mizan says the rhetorical question denies that their equality-claim has revelatory warrant. kitāb is a revealed scripture, tadrusūn means reading it, and takhayyarūn choosing: no divine book tells them they may choose whatever they want, including bliss, in the hereafter.
verses.39: Al-Mizan denies that they possess a divine verbal covenant. Aymān is oaths, and perhaps pacts or covenants; bālighah denotes an oath that reaches fulfillment, possibly lasting until the Resurrection. The rhetorical question exposes as absurd any claim that God has made them a definitive promise granting whatever they demand.
verses.40: Al-Mizan says the challenge is now addressed to the Prophet rather than the polytheists, who no longer merit direct address. A zaʿīm undertakes or oversees a matter, so they are asked who will take responsibility for making them equal to those who submit on the Day of Judgment; with no evidence that God will do this, no one can credibly vouch for it.
verses.41: Al-Mizan reads the associates as alleged partners of God who might intercede for the polytheists and make them equal to those who submit. The command to produce them is rhetorical proof that no such partners exist. Readings that make them fellow believers, witnesses, or sharers in authority are either unsupported or fail to settle the argument; witness-based versions also depend on the already denied book or covenant.
verses.42: Al-Mizan takes yukshafu ʿan sāq, literally the baring of a shank, as a metaphor for an increasingly severe affliction, not a statement about limbs. The parenthetical warning answers the claim of partners and intercessors: happiness in the hereafter is acquired through humble prostration to God in this life. Those who cultivated arrogance will be unable to prostrate then, with lowered eyes and humiliation. "While yet they were safe" may mean that they were secure before the hardships produced by their arrogance, or simply fully able to obey in this world; the interpretation of sujūd as ritual prayer is unsubstantiated.

verses.44: Al-Mizan identifies ḥadīth as the Qur'an: "Leave Me" consoles the Prophet and warns its rejectors that God Himself will deal with them. Istidrāj is their unperceived descent into ruin through repeated blessings: each gift absorbs them, makes them forget gratitude and remembrance, and so becomes the means of destruction rather than a recognized good.
verses.45: Al-Mizan glosses imlāʾ as respite, kayd as stratagem, and matīn as strong. God gives the rejectors time to enlarge the space for further wrongdoing and receive blessings, while His plan remains firm. The shifts from "We" to "I" and then the third person convey grandeur; the singular respite specifically points to extending lifespans, a determination belonging to God alone.
verses.46: Al-Mizan glosses maghram as a fee or debt and muthqalūn as burdened. Linked by am to (68:41), the question asks whether they reject the Prophet's message merely to evade a charge for his prophethood, rather than from conviction.
verses.47: Al-Mizan understands the unseen here as the divine mechanisms of destiny and decree, and "writing" as decreeing. The question therefore asks whether they control fate and can decree equality with those who submit. The alternative that they possess private knowledge and write it down ordinarily is farfetched and ruled out by the preceding possibilities; this remonstration comes last because it is their weakest conceivable ground.
verses.48: Al-Mizan identifies the companion of the fish as Jonah and makẓūm, from kāẓim al-ghayẓ, as anguish or anger choked within a person. The Prophet is told to await God's judgment patiently, without hastening punishment for the rejectors or undergoing Jonah's trial; Jonah's prayer of praise and confession in the fish is recalled at (21:87). The alternative reading of li-ḥukmi rabbika as "towards" God's judgment between the Prophet and his people fits the context less well.
verses.49: Al-Mizan explains niʿmah as accepted repentance, tadārakahu as reaching him, nubidha as cast out, ʿarāʾ as unsheltered open ground, and madhmūm as blamed. Jonah would have been cast out blamed without that grace. This does not conflict with (37:143-144): his continuing glorification prevented his remaining in the fish until Resurrection, whereas accepted repentance prevented his ejection in blame. Together the verses show that his angry departure naturally entailed blame, but divine grace brought release, election, and righteousness; the commentary also recalls its earlier identification of true niʿmah with wilāyah, loyalty to God or the Prophet and his family.
verses.50: Al-Mizan treats ijtibāʾ as choosing and ṣalāḥ as goodness or righteousness.
verses.51: Al-Mizan takes in in wa in yakādu as the light form of inna and yuzliqūnaka as figuratively felling or destroying the Prophet with their eyes. The predominant interpretation is the evil eye, a psychic capacity that reason cannot disprove and narrations support; hateful, killing looks are offered as another reading. Their charge that the Prophet is possessed implies that devils inspired the Qur'an, which its description as a reminder to the nations refutes. The charge repeats the accusation answered at the opening of the sūrah.
